title: Hawke's Bay
description: New Zealand's warm east coast: Bordeaux blends, peppery Syrah and rich Chardonnay.
L: East coast of the North Island

Hawke's Bay lies on the east coast of New Zealand's North Island, around the towns of Napier and Hastings. It's New Zealand's second largest wine region, with about 5,000 hectares. Mountain ranges to the west block rain and wind, and the Pacific is to the east. Soils vary greatly, from river gravels to clay and limestone.

Hawke's Bay is among New Zealand's warmest and sunniest wine regions, which lets later-ripening red grapes ripen. Its maritime climate keeps nights cool and summers moderate. Autumn rain and the occasional cyclone are risks; in 2023, Cyclone Gabrielle flooded many vineyards.
Why can Hawke's Bay ripen Cabernet and Merlot?
It's one of New Zealand's warmest, sunniest regions

Hawke's Bay is one of New Zealand's oldest wine regions: missionaries planted vines in 1851, and Mission Estate is the country's oldest winery still operating. Te Mata Estate, from 1896, helped show from the 1980s that New Zealand could make serious red wine with its Coleraine blend.
Hawke's Bay is New Zealand's largest wine region.
Not true. It's the second largest; Marlborough is the largest.
Hawke's Bay is on the North Island's east coast
It's warm and sunny, sheltered by mountains
Mission Estate, from 1851, is New Zealand's oldest winery

Merlot is the most planted red, with Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc and Malbec, mostly in Bordeaux-style blends. They give medium to full-bodied wines with blackcurrant, plum, cedar and fresh acidity, more elegant than warmer New World examples. Merlot ripens more reliably than Cabernet here.

Syrah does very well: peppery, floral and medium-bodied, closer to the northern Rhône than to Barossa Shiraz. Chardonnay is Hawke's Bay's most planted grape overall, giving ripe yet fresh wines with stone fruit and citrus, often barrel-fermented. Sauvignon Blanc and Pinot Gris also grow.

Explain why it suits red grapes

Gimblett Gravels is an area of about 800 hectares west of Hastings. It's the old bed of the Ngaruroro River, which changed course after a flood in 1867, leaving deep, stony gravel. The land was once considered useless for farming and was nearly quarried for gravel.

The gravel soils drain quickly and store the sun's heat, releasing it at night, making the area a few degrees warmer than its surroundings. Low fertility limits vigour. That helps Cabernet Sauvignon, Merlot and Syrah ripen fully, giving concentrated, structured wines. Irrigation is needed, as the gravel holds little water.
Why does Gimblett Gravels suit red grapes?
Stony soil drains and stores heat

In 2001, producers created the Gimblett Gravels Winegrowing District, defined by soil type rather than political boundaries, a rare approach. Wines labelled Gimblett Gravels must come at least 95% from the district. The Bridge Pa Triangle, nearby, is another warm, red-focused sub-area.
It's low in fertility and drains fast.
Gimblett Gravels is an old riverbed left by an 1867 flood
Stony soil drains and stores heat for red grapes
Its district, from 2001, is defined by soil
Reading Hawke's Bay and eating with it

Labels show the grape or blend, Hawke's Bay GI, and often Gimblett Gravels or Bridge Pa Triangle. Bordeaux blends may list grapes in order of share, like Merlot Cabernet. New Zealand's 85% rules apply. Screw caps are standard, even for reds.

Hawke's Bay Bordeaux blends suit lamb, a New Zealand staple, beef and venison. Syrah suits lamb with rosemary, game and peppered steak. Chardonnay suits roast chicken, crayfish and creamy fish. Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees; good blends age 10 to 15 years.
Which meat is a classic New Zealand match for Hawke's Bay reds?
New Zealand lamb suits its Bordeaux blends and Syrah.
